normal_signature: Axial cross-section of a human brain with bilateral symmetry
Presence of dark, butterfly-shaped lateral ventricles in the center
Distinct contrast between grey matter (cortex) and white matter
Intact, continuous outer boundary of the brain tissue
Absence of large, irregular hyperintense (bright) lesions
Do not classify symmetric periventricular hyperintensities as anomalies if they appear bilaterally in the same anatomical region.
If ventricle morphology is symmetric and tissue texture is uniform, classify as normal even if subtle periventricular hyperintensities are present.
If initial visual inspection finds no candidate anomalous features, cap the final anomaly score at 0.25 to reflect high confidence in normality.
Do not flag dark, fluid-filled ventricular structures in the brain's center as anomalies; these are normal anatomical features.
Do not classify symmetric, bilateral ring-like hyperintensities in deep brain structures as anomalies; these are normal anatomical features.
hypothesized_anomaly_modes: Ischemic stroke or infarction causing focal bright lesions in the white matter
Brain tumor presenting as a mass effect distorting the ventricles or midline
Severe atrophy resulting in enlarged ventricles and widened sulci
Hemorrhage appearing as a distinct, irregular dark or bright spot depending on age
Artifact corruption such as motion blur or signal dropout obscuring anatomical details
Flag as anomaly if a large, heterogeneous mass with irregular borders and significant mass effect is present.
If a focal hyperintense lesion is detected in the posterior hemisphere, override refutation and classify as anomaly.
If a large hyperintense mass is detected in the cerebral hemisphere, immediately classify as anomaly regardless of initial uncertainty.
If a large, irregular hyperintense mass with surrounding edema is detected, override any refutation and classify as anomaly.
If a focal hyperintense lesion is detected in the periventricular region and absent in normal references, classify as anomaly.
rules: if the image shows a large, irregular bright spot (hyperintensity) in the brain tissue that is not part of the ventricles, then lean anomaly
if the lateral ventricles are significantly distorted, shifted, or asymmetrical, then lean anomaly
if the brain tissue boundary is jagged, incomplete, or shows severe signal dropout, then lean anomaly
if the image displays clear bilateral symmetry with distinct grey/white matter differentiation and no focal lesions, then lean normal
if the ventricles are clearly visible and maintain a standard butterfly shape without mass effect, then lean normal
